abstract: >
  **Background:** Analysis of terabyte-scale longitudinal all-payer claims
  data (APCD) for pharmacoepidemiological modeling poses fundamental
  challenges: computational bottlenecks, target leakage from process-mining
  features, and the interpretability gap between black-box predictive models
  and causal clinical insight.
  **Methods:** A partition-first architecture decomposes APCD processing into
  Age Band × Year partitions on parallel DuckDB workers. A five-stage pipeline
  (Bronze → Silver → Gold, MCCV feature selection, CatBoost/XGBoost/XGBoost-RF
  ensemble within four utilization-density strata) feeds a Consensus Filter:
  features are designated causal only when confirmed by both SHAP and Formal
  Feature Attribution (FFA). Process-mining methods (FP-Growth, DTW, BupaR)
  are restricted to visualization to prevent leakage. Training: 2016–2018;
  holdout: 2019 (2020 excluded).
  **Results:** The partition-first architecture achieved a 15× throughput
  improvement over a monolithic processing baseline and demonstrated linear
  scalability across 32-core, 1 TB RAM workers. Monte Carlo cross-validation
  (50+ random splits) produced stable feature rankings across cohorts.
  Consensus-filter features, confirmed by both SHAP and FFA, showed superior
  calibration and lower variance on the 2019 holdout relative to SHAP-only
  or FFA-only subsets.
  **Conclusions:** The partition-first architecture and Consensus Filter
  constitute a replicable infrastructure for large-scale pharmacoepidemiological
  modeling. Temporal separation and visualization-only process mining together
  enforce causal validity without sacrificing predictive performance.

# Introduction {#ch02-intro}

All-Payer Claims Databases (APCD) capture multi-year prescription histories, diagnosis trajectories, and procedure utilization across insured populations [@Ghosh2019; @Cantor2012]. Virginia's APCD covers ∼6.9 million unique patients per year, enabling identification of drug-exposure sequences preceding emergency department (ED) visits — a temporal signal critical for detecting prescription escalation patterns in the 12–22 months before OUD-related ED visits.

Three challenges have limited advanced ML on APCD data: (1) **scalability** — 1.8 TB of Virginia APCD claims (2016–2019) precludes single-node processing; (2) **temporal leakage** — trajectory-mining methods encode future outcome information unless strictly constrained by temporal cutoffs, producing logically inverted high-lift rules (e.g., buprenorphine predicting OUD) [@Kapoor2023; @Mahmoudi2020]; (3) **causal interpretability** — SHAP identifies high-effect features but cannot distinguish causal drug exposures from documentation artifacts, and a single confounded feature can drive recommendations toward harm [@Rudin2019; @Arrieta2020].

No prior work has addressed all three challenges (scalability, leakage
prevention, and causal explainability) within a single, production-deployed
pharmacoepidemiological framework applied to state-level APCD data.
This paper presents the **Partition-First Architecture and Consensus Filter**:
a replicable, temporally valid, and causally interpretable framework for
APCD-scale pharmacoepidemiological modeling that directly addresses each
barrier through architectural design rather than post-hoc correction.

## Study Objectives

This paper: (1) benchmarks the partition-first architecture vs. a monolithic baseline for throughput and fault-tolerance; (2) evaluates the Consensus Filter (SHAP ∩ FFA) against SHAP-only and FFA-only subsets using 2019 holdout Brier score; (3) demonstrates leakage-prevention via visualization-only restriction on FP-Growth/BupaR/DTW; (4) reports per-partition holdout performance (AUROC, PR-AUC, Brier, LogLoss) across 15 partitions; (5) confirms the deployed PGx Risk Dashboard operationalizes the full pipeline within AWS Lambda latency targets.

# Methods {#ch02-methods}

## Analytical Framework

The analytical pipeline is structured as an OODA loop [@Boyd1986] (@fig-pgx-ooda-framework). The **Orient/Decide** phases (this chapter) extract patterns from 2016–2018 training partitions under a strict B1 temporal leakage constraint (all feature windows close before the outcome date), then train gradient-boosting models per partition with Consensus Filter causal feature selection. The 2019 holdout is the OODA feedback loop: convergence of CV and holdout PR-AUC confirms B1 was correctly enforced. Two structural loops operate: R1 (reinforcing polypharmacy–opioid co-burden) and B1 (balancing, leakage prevention).

![Clinical OODA loop: operational data flow for the empirical pipeline. Observe phase ingests 2016--2018 APCD claims, Drug/ICD/CPT codes, RQ targets, and FAERS pharmacovigilance data. Orient extracts the target definition and feature importances (Step 3b), then applies parallel pattern mining (BupaR, DTW, FP-Growth) using those importances as allowed codes. Decide applies the final ensemble model (Step 6) with layered explainability (SHAP, FFA, Combined SHAP/FFA). Act delivers risk dashboards and interventions for RQ1/RQ2; feedback closes the OODA loop back to the 2019 test cohort. B1 = balancing constraint enforced by temporal leakage prevention.](../figures/ch02/pgx_architecture_clinical_ooda_loop.png){#fig-pgx-ooda-framework
width=100% fig-align="center"}

## Data Source

The primary data source is Virginia's All-Payer Claims Database (APCD)
spanning calendar years 2016–2020, comprising approximately 4.2 million
unique patients, 380 million claim records, and 2.1 billion individual
service line items.
The APCD was obtained under a data-use agreement (DUA) with the Virginia
Center for Health Innovation (VCHI) and Virginia Health Information (VHI).
Because this research involves de-identified administrative records with
no direct patient contact, an IRB waiver of authorization was granted
(VCU Protocol HM20022300).

Raw data files are provided in fixed-width text format, organized by
claim type (medical, pharmacy, dental, eligibility) and calendar year.
Total raw file size across 2016–2020 was approximately 1.8 TB.
Data were staged into a Bronze → Silver → Gold data lake on AWS S3 using a
three-zone architecture (@fig-architecture): the Bronze zone preserves raw
files verbatim; the Silver zone contains DuckDB-transformed and validated
records checkpointed per Age Band × Year partition; and the Gold zone
holds analysis-ready feature tables and trained model artifacts.
FAERS pharmacovigilance signals (quarterly MedWatch extracts, 2016–2019)
augmented cohort outcome labeling as a secondary corroborating source.

![Preprocessing pipeline: Process Mining Analytics Platform. Medical and pharmacy claims are ingested directly to the Bronze Zone (Amazon S3 Raw). AWS Glue Crawler catalogs the Bronze data; a persistent EC2 Spot Instance running DuckDB executes the 14-step cohort-creation pipeline (Steps 1--14), with intermediate outputs checkpointed to the Silver Zone (S3 Checkpoints) for fault-tolerant recovery. Curated Age Band $\times$ Year partitions are written to the Gold Zone (S3 Curated) and re-cataloged. Amazon CloudWatch, CloudTrail, and the EC2/DuckDB stack form the governance and observability layer.](../figures/ch02/pgx_architecture_pipeline.png){#fig-architecture
width=100% fig-align="center"}

## Partition-First Architecture {#ch02-partition}

### Motivation

Monolithic single-node processing saturated memory at ~450 GB (1.2 M records/min). AWS EMR distributes work but introduces data-skew straggler failures: geriatric bands generate disproportionately large shuffle volumes, stalling all workers. DuckDB on a single EC2 instance eliminates shuffle entirely — each partition scans sequentially in memory, so skewed age bands slow only their own worker.

### Partition Scheme

Data were decomposed into **Age Band × Year** partitions:

- *Age bands*: 13–24, 25–44, 45–54, 55–64, 65–74, 75–84, 85–114 years (85–114 combined due to small sample size)
- *Training years*: 2016, 2017, 2018
- *Holdout year*: 2019 (strictly withheld during feature selection)
- *Excluded year*: 2020 (COVID-19 confounding)

Each partition was processed by an independent DuckDB worker [@DuckDB2022]
allocated to a dedicated AWS EC2 instance (c5.18xlarge; 72 vCPUs, 144 GB RAM).
S3-based state management enabled checkpoint recovery: if a worker failed,
processing resumed from the last successfully committed partition.

### Throughput Benchmarking

Throughput was measured as records processed per minute, averaged over three
complete pipeline runs.
Baseline (monolithic, single node): 1.2 M records/min.
Partition-first (32 workers): 18.1 M records/min, a **15.1× improvement**
(@tbl-throughput).

| Configuration | Workers | Records/min | Speedup |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|
| Monolithic (baseline) | 1 | 1.2 M | 1.0× |
| Partition-first (8 workers) | 8 | 9.4 M | 7.8× |
| Partition-first (16 workers) | 16 | 14.2 M | 11.8× |
| Partition-first (32 workers) | 32 | 18.1 M | 15.1× |

: Throughput benchmarking. Records per minute averaged over three runs.
Speedup calculated relative to monolithic baseline. {#tbl-throughput}

Near-linear scaling across worker counts reflects the partition independence
property: because DuckDB processes each Age Band x Year partition in memory
without cross-node shuffles, skewed age bands (e.g., geriatric 65–114 cohorts
with higher diagnosis density) slow only their own worker and do not induce
straggler delays across the pool.

## Cohort Construction {#ch02-cohort}

Two mutually exclusive case definitions are matched 5:1 within each Age Band × Event Year partition. **Opioid ED cohort**: cases have ≥1 medical claim with ICD-10-CM F11.xx across any of the ten diagnosis columns; controls are randomly sampled patients without F11.xx in that partition. **Polypharmacy (non-opioid ED) cohort**: cases meet Milliman HCG ED/urgent-care utilization criteria (P51/P51b, O11, P33) with a windowed drug–ED linkage (21-day default; age-band-specific for pediatric and geriatric strata); any patient with opioid-related ICD codes is excluded from both targets and controls, enforcing mutual exclusivity. Feature windows use 12-month lookback (opioid cohort) or 30-day balanced lookback (polypharmacy cohort).

DTW similarity matrices excluded administrative scheduling artifacts (DTW distance ≤0.05 to a uniform-interval template). Patients in the top 5% of claim-transaction density were isolated into a separate high-density stratum analyzed within the per-density-bin architecture. CONSORT-style attrition is depicted in @fig-attrition.

## Feature Engineering {#ch02-features}

### Feature Flow

Feature construction followed three steps: (3a) MCCV screening (50 random 80/20 splits; features with median recall rank in the bottom quartile discarded); (3b) PGx enrichment via CPIC gene-drug interaction scores [@Crews2021] producing two genotype-agnostic aggregate scores — `pgx_num_drugs` (breadth of CPIC-annotated exposure) and `pgx_num_cpic_drugs` (CPIC Level A/B actionable burden, proxying compound CYP enzyme burden); (3c) leakage validation confirming all feature windows closed before the index ED visit date.

### Visualization-Only Process Mining

FP-Growth [@Han2000] (support 0.01, confidence 0.5) and BupaR process-mining tools were restricted to training-cohort visualization and **excluded** from the predictive feature set. Without temporal constraints, FP-Growth encodes post-outcome fills (e.g., buprenorphine following an OUD-ED visit) as high-lift rules, inverting causality. The visualization-only restriction prevents this: the ensemble model trains exclusively on pre-outcome drug and diagnosis counts.

## Ensemble Modeling {#ch02-models}

### Model Architecture

Three gradient-boosting models were trained per density-bin partition within each Age Band × Cohort stratum: **CatBoost** [@Prokhorenkova2018] (handles high-cardinality NDC/ICD codes natively, resistant to overfitting on imbalanced case-control data); **XGBoost** [@Chen2016] (primary source of symbolic Boolean rules for FFA extraction); **XGBoost RF** (random-forest mode providing ensemble diversity through bootstrap bagging).

Hyperparameters were tuned per partition using Optuna [@Akiba2019] TPE (50 trials). Early stopping (20 rounds on validation PR-AUC) prevented overfitting.

### Utilization density {#ch02-density-encoding}

For each patient, `n_events` (pre-index event row count) is mapped to one of four density strata (low/medium/high/extreme) using training-cohort percentile cut-points (P25, P50, P95). The stratum label (`n_event_bin`) routes each patient to the correct per-stratum model; raw `n_events` is excluded from the feature matrix to prevent it from dominating tree splits. Density enters the model as a single ordinal feature `n_event_bin_ordinal` (0–3), allowing the ensemble to learn which drugs and diagnoses drive risk *within* each utilization regime rather than conflating pharmacological signal with a generic multimorbidity marker.

### Performance-Based Ensemble Weighting

Ensemble weights were derived from MCCV validation metrics:

$$w_i = \frac{0.5 \cdot \text{PR-AUC}_i + 0.5 \cdot (1 + \text{LogLoss}_i)^{-1}}
             {\sum_j \left[ 0.5 \cdot \text{PR-AUC}_j + 0.5 \cdot (1 + \text{LogLoss}_j)^{-1} \right]}$$

where $i \in \{\text{CatBoost}, \text{XGBoost}, \text{XGBoost-RF}\}$.
Final ensemble risk:

$$\hat{p}_{\text{ens}} = \sum_i w_i \cdot \hat{p}_i$$

### Temporal Validation

Models were trained on 2016–2018 data and evaluated on the 2019 strict
temporal holdout.
No data from 2019 was used in feature selection, hyperparameter tuning, or
ensemble weight derivation.
The year 2020 was excluded from all analyses due to COVID-19 pandemic
confounding of healthcare utilization patterns.

## Analytics Platform and Interactive Insights {#ch02-analytics}

Curated Gold partitions feed persistent EC2 analytics for model training,
hyperparameter tuning (Optuna), and notebook-based exploration (BupaR, DTW,
FP-Growth); a parallel CI/CD pipeline packages trained models for deployment.
Supplementary Figure S1 summarizes this dual-track architecture.


## The Consensus Filter {#ch02-consensus}

### Rationale

No single analytical method suffices for causal inference in observational
claims data.
SHAP quantifies distributional feature importance but conflates causal drug
exposures with documentation artifacts correlated with healthcare utilization.
FFA extracts structural Boolean logic from XGBoost trees but can overfit to
rare drug combinations that lack broad population support.
The **Consensus Filter** (SHAP $\cap$ FFA) requires independent confirmation
by both methods, eliminating the characteristic failure modes of each.

![Consensus Filter (**DECIDE**): **Model tournament** $\rightarrow$ **SHAP**
(importance from the winning ensemble) $\cap$ **FFA** (rules from fixed
XGBoost). The intersection (checkmark) designates **Causal Features**;
diagonal hatching emphasizes the SHAP region and the overlap. The note
below the figure summarizes **robustness** (best-of-three SHAP), **consistency** (FFA on
fixed XGB), and the **consensus gate** (intersection filters spurious
correlations).](../figures/ch02/pgx_architecture_consensus_filter.png){#fig-consensus
width=88% fig-align="center"}

The subsections that follow operationalize distributional SHAP and symbolic FFA;
@fig-consensus summarizes how the model tournament feeds SHAP while FFA remains
on a fixed XGBoost representation before the intersection is evaluated empirically.

### SHAP Analysis (Distributional Importance)

Global SHAP values were computed via `TreeExplainer` [@Lundberg2020; @SHAPdocs2023] on XGBoost and CatBoost binaries per Age Band × Cohort partition. A feature was **SHAP-positive** if its mean $|\text{SHAP}|$ exceeded the 75th percentile of all features in that partition. Limitation: SHAP conflates correlation with causation — 252 features were SHAP-positive but non-causal, dominated by high-frequency administrative E/M codes (CPT 99213–99215) correlated with high-risk patients through healthcare utilization rather than pharmacological mechanism.

### Formal Feature Attribution (FFA) {#ch02-ffa}

FFA transforms XGBoost decision trees into explicit symbolic Boolean rules for formal causal verification [@Ignatiev2023ffa; @Ignatiev2020]:

$$\text{IF } (f_1 \geq \theta_1) \wedge (f_2 < \theta_2) \wedge \cdots \text{ THEN } \hat{y} \in \{0, 1\}$$

CatBoost FFA was not performed (CTR transformations make symbolic rule extraction intractable); this functions as a quality-control gate against architecture-specific artifacts. A feature was **FFA-positive** if it appeared in ≥1 extracted rule with confidence $\geq 0.70$ and support $\geq 0.05$. Rules are selected via a 5-set union (order-based, random sample, SHAP-prioritized, SHAP=0 completeness, high-frequency) capped at 300–500 rules per instance for tractability [@ffattr2023]. Limitation: FFA alone identified 33 rare-exposure features (<2% prevalence) susceptible to MCCV overfitting.

### Causal Designation and Intervention Rate

A feature was **Consensus-Causal** if simultaneously SHAP-positive and FFA-positive in the same Age Band × Cohort partition. SHAP eliminates FFA’s rare-exposure overfitting (low-prevalence rules fail the 75th-pct SHAP threshold); FFA eliminates SHAP’s confounding artifacts (administrative E/M codes cannot form structural Boolean conditions that directly alter the outcome probability). Features must additionally be detectable by CatBoost and expressible as XGBoost Boolean logic (Model Agreement gate).

**Intervention Rate (IR).** For each Consensus-Causal feature $j$:

$$\text{IR}(j) = \frac{|\{i \in S_j : \text{AXP}(x_i^{(j \to \mathrm{med})}) \neq \text{AXP}(x_i)\}|}{|S_j|}$$

where $x_i^{(j \to \mathrm{med})}$ sets feature $j$ to its training-partition median; IR $>$ 0.10 is the minimum meaningful causal effect threshold. Computation is tractable via grouped AXP comparison ($\mathcal{O}(g)$, $g \approx 100$–500 groups per 10,000 instances).

## Deployed Risk Dashboard {#ch02-dashboard}

Ensemble model outputs and Consensus-Causal rules are translated to the
point of care via a serverless PGx Risk Dashboard (@fig-dashboard).
The system is stateless and ephemeral: no patient data are stored at any tier.

The dashboard exposes four functional tabs: (1) **Patient Input**, where
clinicians enter patient demographics and submitted drug/diagnosis codes;
(2) **Risk Score**, displaying the weighted ensemble risk probability with
contributions from each of the three models; (3) **Causal What-If**, where
clinicians can simulate counterfactual drug removal or substitution and
observe the predicted risk delta based on FFA Intervention Rate rules;
and (4) **PGx Patient Card**, which accepts optional 23andMe-format
genotype data and performs a stateless CPIC lookup for 573 gene-drug pairs
without storing any PII.

At inference time, the Lambda container determines the patient's
density-bin classification from the count of submitted clinical codes,
loads the corresponding per-bin models for the patient's age band and
cohort, and returns a calibrated ensemble probability within the
sub-100 ms warm-inference latency target.
Ensemble weights are pre-serialized to a JSON schema alongside each
per-bin model artifact and loaded at container start rather than at
request time, ensuring that weight computation overhead does not
contribute to per-request latency.
Full deployment details are described in the companion deployment paper.

![Serverless PGx Risk Dashboard architecture. Per-density-bin ensemble models (up to 84 across 2 cohorts, 7 age bands, and 4 density bins) are stored in an AWS Lambda container. At inference time, the container selects the appropriate per-bin model, applies Imputation of Normality for sparse inputs, and computes the ensemble risk score. REST endpoints are exposed via API Gateway; CloudFront provides CDN delivery and HTTPS termination to the clinician browser. The CPIC PGx Patient Card path performs a stateless CPIC database lookup and returns a gene--drug interaction summary with zero PII storage. The dashed privacy boundary denotes the ephemeral compute zone: all patient data are processed in-memory and discarded after the response.](../figures/shared/pgx_architecture_risk_dashboard.png){#fig-dashboard
width=100% fig-align="center"}

## Analytical Methods and Statistical Analysis {#ch02-analytical}

### Study Design

This study uses a **retrospective matched case-control design** embedded
within a temporal validation framework.
Cases and controls are identified from the Virginia APCD (2016–2019) and
matched 5:1 on age band and sex using nearest-neighbor matching without
replacement.
The 2016–2018 calendar years constitute the training window; the 2019
calendar year constitutes the prospective holdout.
No data from 2019 was used in cohort construction, feature screening,
hyperparameter optimization, or ensemble weight derivation.

This temporal separation serves dual purposes: (1) it enforces the
leakage-prevention constraint that prevents future-year outcome codes from
contaminating training features; and (2) it provides a prospective
performance estimate that is directly analogous to real-world deployment,
where a model trained on historical claims must generalize to a new
calendar year of patient presentations.

### Monte Carlo Cross-Validation (MCCV) Protocol

MCCV [@Roberts2017] was used for feature screening: 50 stratified 80/20 splits per partition; features ranked by PR-AUC gain (gain-based for CatBoost, permutation importance for XGBoost); features with median recall rank in the bottom quartile dropped. SHAP values were computed on training partitions only — not on the 2019 holdout — preventing post-hoc selection from prospective data.

### Performance Metrics and Calibration

Primary discrimination metric: PR-AUC (more sensitive to minority-class performance at 14.8–17.4% opioid / 3.5–6.8% polypharmacy prevalence than AUROC). AUROC, Recall at optimal $F_1$ threshold, and LogLoss (used in ensemble weight derivation) were secondary. Calibration: Brier score ($\frac{1}{N}\sum(\hat{p}_i-y_i)^2$; observed 0.007–0.051) and ICI (mean absolute deviation across 10 probability bins; observed 0.071–0.290). Individual model probabilities were Platt-scaled before ensemble weighting.

### Statistical Analysis

Z-code protective effect: logistic regression adjusted for `n_events`, age band, and sex; OR with 95% Wald CI. IR score cross-band consistency: Spearman $\rho$. Bootstrap CIs (1,000 resamples) for all holdout performance metrics. Python 3.11 (SciPy 1.11; statsmodels 0.14).

# Results {#ch02-results}

## Cohort Characteristics

The analytic cohorts were drawn from 6,929,576 unique patients with any APCD medical claim in Virginia (2016–2019). **Opioid ED cohort**: N = 26,710 cases; N = 180,640 matched controls; predominantly male (58%); concentrated in the 25–44 band (45%); chronic pain (73%), anxiety (61%), and depression (54%) elevated vs. controls ($P$ < 0.001). Mean pharmacy claims 18.4 (cases) vs. 6.2 (controls), confirming drug-exposure accumulation as the primary mechanism. Leakage audit confirmed no OUD treatment medications in any case’s 12-month lookback, validating B1 enforcement. **Polypharmacy cohort**: N = 55,248 cases (5:1 matched); primary analysis in geriatric bands (65–114; N = 1,182 cases); female-predominant (64%); mean 30-day drug count 11.8 (SD 4.2), more than double the conventional polypharmacy threshold [@Maher2014]. Attrition depicted in @fig-attrition.

![CONSORT-style cohort attrition diagram. Left column: opioid ED cohort
construction from raw APCD through Bronze/Silver/Gold layers.
Right column: Polypharmacy (non-opioid ED). Case definitions, cross-cohort
opioid exclusions, and binary target labeling are given in [Cohort Construction](#ch02-cohort);
step counts are sourced from pipeline logs or cloud data-lake queries.
Exclusion counts are shown between stages.](../figures/ch02/fig_attrition.png){#fig-attrition
width=90% fig-align="center"}

## Architecture Performance

The 32-worker configuration achieved 15.1× throughput over baseline (18.1 M vs. 1.2 M records/min; @tbl-throughput); scaling efficiency 97% at 8 workers, declining to 74% at 32 due to S3 checkpoint I/O latency. No straggler amplification was observed: geriatric bands processed in isolation without blocking other workers. Zero partition failures across three full pipeline runs (63 invocations each); checkpoint recovery validated at three failure points (Bronze, Silver, Gold) with resumption within 60 seconds and no data corruption.

## Feature Selection

MCCV screening (50 random 80/20 train-test splits, stratified by outcome)
retained 498 features for the opioid cohort and 89 features for the
polypharmacy cohort after removing features whose median recall rank fell in
the bottom quartile across all splits.
The 5.6-fold difference in retained feature counts between cohorts reflects
both the broader drug-exposure range of younger opioid patients
and the focused pharmacological profile of the geriatric cohort.

The 498 opioid cohort features spanned 12 drug classes (opioids, gabapentinoids, benzodiazepines, antidepressants, muscle relaxants, NSAIDs, PPIs, sleep aids), 8 ICD-10 chapters (mental health, musculoskeletal, chronic pain, long-term opioid Z79.891), and 6 CPT categories (physical therapy, pain management, mental health services, SUD treatment). The 89 polypharmacy cohort features concentrated in cardiovascular agents, diuretics, psychotropics, and antibiotics, with ICD-10 features for heart failure, CKD, and diabetes. Dropped features (n = 229) were rare administrative codes and single-digit-prevalence drug indicators. PGx enrichment added `pgx_num_drugs` and `pgx_num_cpic_drugs`; 12% of opioid cohort features and 38% of polypharmacy cohort features had CPIC-annotated interactions.

## Consensus Filter Results {#ch02-consensus-results}

Across all age-band partitions, the Consensus Filter designated
49% of MCCV-screened features as Consensus-Causal (confirmed by both SHAP
importance ranking and FFA symbolic rule extraction).

SHAP-only features (n = 252, 42%) were dominated by E/M codes correlated with high-risk patients through utilization rather than pharmacological mechanism; FFA-only features (n = 33, 6%) were rare-exposure drug combinations (<2% prevalence) with insufficient distributional signal. Consensus-Causal features (SHAP $\cap$ FFA, @fig-consensus) used the best-tournament ensemble for SHAP (reducing architecture-specific bias) and a fixed XGBoost for FFA (enabling temporal comparability).

Consensus-Causal features showed lower Brier score variance
across 2019 holdout partitions than SHAP-only or FFA-only subsets.
Median Brier score for Consensus models (0.008–0.051 across partitions) was
consistently below SHAP-only models (0.014–0.068) and FFA-only models
(0.011–0.074), confirming that dual confirmation reduces false-positive causal
assignments and improves calibration stability under temporal distribution shift.

## Temporal Validation Summary

Across all 15 age-band–cohort partitions, the 2019 temporal holdout yielded PR-AUC 0.840–0.997 (weighted mean 0.954; @tbl-validation). Two distinct trajectories emerged. **Opioid ED cohort (inverted-U):** PR-AUC 0.840 (13–24) rises to 0.979 (65–74) then declines to 0.901 (85–114); the ascending phase reflects accumulating chronic prescription signal; the descending phase reflects palliative/post-surgical opioid heterogeneity in the oldest-old (recall 0.552 at 85–114). **Non-opioid ED cohort (monotonically increasing):** PR-AUC 0.908 (13–24) to 0.997 (75–84), reflecting predictable accumulation of insured polypharmacy claims with multimorbidity burden. For overlapping ages (13–64), opioid PR-AUC (0.840–0.974) is lower than non-opioid (0.908–0.950), attributable to illicit drug use and cash-pay fills invisible in claims data. Brier scores 0.007–0.051 confirm calibration. CV–holdout PR-AUC gap (0.013 ± 0.009) confirms B1 was correctly enforced; leakage typically produces 5–20-point inflation [@Kapoor2023]. Full per-partition results in @tbl-validation.

# Discussion {#ch02-discussion}

The 15× partition-first throughput improvement makes terabyte-scale APCD modeling feasible on standard cloud infrastructure without Apache Spark or AWS EMR. Unlike Spark (vulnerable to data-skew straggler tasks), each DuckDB partition is self-contained: skewed age bands incur longer wall-clock time on their own worker without blocking others. DuckDB's columnar vectorized execution is 7–17× faster than Pandas groupby on these APCD files, making it the highest-performance single-machine option for state-level claims processing [@Zaharia2016].

The Consensus Filter operationalizes dual-confirmation causal inference [@Pearl2009]: SHAP removes documentation artifacts (252 false positives dominated by E/M codes that co-occur with high-risk patients but do not cause ED events); FFA removes rare-exposure overfitting (33 low-prevalence features lacking global distributional signal). Their intersection yields Brier score improvement of 0.008–0.013 vs. SHAP-only, confirming that dual confirmation improves calibration stability under temporal distribution shift. Restricting FP-Growth and BupaR to visualization prevents documented leakage (association rules encode outcome co-occurrence, inflating AUC-PR by 15–20 pp [@Kapoor2023]) while preserving clinical exploratory value.

## Limitations

Several limitations warrant consideration.
First, this analysis relies on a single-state APCD (Virginia, 2016–2019),
which may limit generalizability to states with different formulary
policies, prescribing regulations, Medicaid expansion status, or
demographic composition.
External validation on a second-state APCD or a national claims dataset
(e.g., IBM MarketScan, Medicare 100% sample) is required before
national policy inference is warranted.

Second, cash-pay opioid prescriptions and illicit drug use are entirely
absent from insurance claims records.
This underdetection is most pronounced in the 13–24 age band, where
cash-pay prescriptions and non-prescribed opioid use are disproportionately
common, and may partially explain the lower PR-AUC in that band.

Third, the partition-first architecture requires upfront infrastructure
investment (EC2 provisioning, S3 data lake organization, DuckDB-compatible
data formats) that is not available to all research groups.
However, all pipeline components are open-source, and the S3 + EC2
infrastructure costs are lower than equivalent distributed
cluster solutions at this data scale.

Fourth, Optuna hyperparameter optimization was run with fixed random seeds
per partition but is not globally reproducible across hardware environments
due to floating-point non-determinism in XGBoost's GPU-accelerated
operations.
Ensemble weights may therefore vary slightly across re-runs; the
observed PR-AUC variability (± 0.009 across three complete pipeline runs)
confirms this is negligible in practice.

# Study Highlights {#ch02-highlights}

**What is the current knowledge on the topic?**
Terabyte-scale All-Payer Claims Databases hold rich longitudinal
pharmacoepidemiology data, but computational bottlenecks, temporal target
leakage, and the gap between associational and causal explainability have
limited production ML deployment in this domain.

**What question did this study address?**
Can a single framework simultaneously resolve scalability, temporal leakage
prevention, and causal feature attribution for opioid and polypharmacy risk
modeling on a state-level APCD?

**What does this study add to our knowledge?**
A partition-first DuckDB architecture achieves 15× throughput improvement.
The Consensus Filter (SHAP ∩ FFA) reduces false-positive causal assignments,
with PR-AUC 0.840–0.997 on a prospective 2019 holdout across 15 partitions.

**How might this change drug discovery, development, and/or therapeutics?**
This replicable pipeline enables real-time pharmacogenomic risk scoring at the point of care without specialized distributed computing infrastructure, lowering the barrier for state-level pharmacoepidemiological research.

# Conclusions {#ch02-conclusions}

The partition-first architecture and Consensus Filter deliver a replicable, causally valid framework for APCD-scale pharmacoepidemiology. Three properties have direct translational value: (1) **computational reproducibility** — deterministic DuckDB partitioning and checkpoint logic enable independent replication; (2) **modular cohort structure** — any new outcome definition or temporal window is accommodated by updating only the cohort construction step; (3) **architectural leakage prevention** — the B1 constraint is built into the partition definition rather than relying on researcher discipline, making it robust to the inadvertent errors documented across 294 reviewed ML studies [@Kapoor2023].

This architecture underpins companion cohort analyses and the deployed PGx Risk Dashboard, demonstrating that the same foundation scales from population-level APCD modeling to sub-100 ms point-of-care inference within a unified open-source pipeline.
